For the training dynamics figure, there's a clear contrast between exception-only converging quickly to ~99.83% and full-trace oscillating between 82-89% without stable convergence, though there's an inconsistency between the caption saying "Full-trace with label-only loss" and the legend just saying "Full Trace."

Looking more closely at the red line's peak of ~88.82%, this doesn't match the final full_trace accuracy of 81.76% or the label_only mean of 85.94%, but it's closer to label_only's range—suggesting the figure might be showing peak evaluation accuracy during training rather than final performance, which creates ambiguity about what condition is actually being visualized.

The caption explicitly states "Full-trace with label-only loss," which describes the label_only condition, but the figure legend just says "Full Trace"—this mismatch is a significant labeling inconsistency that could mislead readers about which experimental condition is shown.

The budget curve clearly demonstrates the phase transition between 384 and 512 tokens, with all four model lines converging around 93-98% accuracy at 512+ tokens, and the reference baselines are well-marked. The calibration figure appears to be starting with four subplots.

Now I'm looking at the calibration results more carefully. The reliability diagrams show that exception_only and VOTA maintain good calibration while no_trace and full_trace are poorly calibrated, which is a professional visualization. I think I have enough to start writing the review.

The core novelty concern is that exception events inherently contain the test verdict signal—when tests fail, it's typically because an exception was raised, including AssertionErrors from test assertions. While the paper notes that 55.5% of failures are silent logic errors, these still produce AssertionErrors, so the exception_only representation essentially captures what the test framework already signals. The actual learning contribution through SFT rather than simple regex matching appears relatively limited.

The 24%/76% information decomposition is derived from a single model with three seeds and uses approximate calculations, which limits its impact. The training dynamics comparison also seems somewhat unfair since exception_only inputs are around 150 tokens median while full_trace exceeds 2000 tokens—faster convergence on simpler inputs is naturally expected.

There's a significant motivation gap here. In CI/CD pipelines, test frameworks already report pass/fail directly, and while the paper mentions potential applications like patch correctness prediction and flaky test detection in the discussion, there's no actual validation of these use cases. The practical scenario remains unclear: if you're running the test to get traces, you already have the verdict.

The framing around "richer traces actively hurt" is confounded by the 2048-token truncation limit, though the paper does acknowledge this. The title also feels like it's following a tired convention. On the positive side, the experiments are thorough across multiple models and seeds with rigorous statistical reporting including confidence intervals and bootstrap analysis. The information density framework itself is novel, and the budget curve analysis effectively identifies that ~500-token phase transition. The ablations without format markers and regex baselines also convincingly address concerns about format artifacts. There are some minor inconsistencies though—Figure 3's legend says "Full Trace" while the caption refers to "Full-trace with label-only loss"—and the abstract is quite data-heavy.

The submission meets all formatting requirements: 8 pages, anonymous, limitations and ethics sections included, ARR checklist provided separately. The related work covers execution traces, verdict classification, fault localization, and trace compression across 54 references, though it could be more explicit about test result parsing and code agents. Most references check out, though about 8 entries from 2025-2026 aren't yet in OpenAlex.

On the core evaluation: the methodology is sound but the central finding—that exception events predict test outcomes—feels somewhat tautological, limiting the novelty. The work shows statistical rigor and the training dynamics analysis adds some value, but the practical motivation is weak and the decomposition only covers one model. This lands it at a 3.0 overall, solid empirical work that's competent but not particularly exciting.
```

You Need\" (2017) 以来，此标题模式在 ML 论文中被大量使用，已成为 reviewer 疲劳点。此标题同时暗示了一种绝对性的 claim（\"all you need\"），而论文本身的 Limitations 列出了 8 项限制条件。\n- 建议：考虑更精确的标题，如 \"Exception Events Dominate Trace-Based Verdict Prediction: A Component Ablation Study\"。\n\n---\n\n## 小问题（不影响接收）\n\n- Section 2.2 (method.tex line 12)：数据集描述中 \"10 candidate solutions per problem from Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct\" 与 Limitations 第五点（\"candidate solutions were generated by Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, which also serves as one of our evaluation models\"）构成 generator-evaluator overlap，虽已承认，但可在 Method section 更早提及。\n- Appendix C (VOTA Extraction Algorithm)：Algorithm 1 line 8 的 \"[No exception data in trace]\" marker 是 pass/fail 信号的 near-deterministic indicator（regex B5 = 99.33%），应在正文首次提到 exception_only 表示时就明确这一设计选择。\n- Table 1 caption 过长（约 6 行），包含了大量 footnote-level 的信息（如 DeepSeek outlier 的处理、VOTA 3-seed results 等），建议精简 caption 并将细节移至正文或 footnote。\n- Appendix 中某些 Table 的 caption（如 Table 12, 13）引用了 main text section 编号（如 §F），应使用 Appendix section label 以避免编号不一致。\n- references.bib 中 `qwen2025coder` 的 key 写 2025 但 year=2024，建议统一。\n\n---\n\n## 缺失引用\n\n论文 Related Work 覆盖面尚可（54 条引用，6 个方向），但以下方向覆盖不足：\n\n1. **Test result parsing / build log analysis**: 论文将 verdict prediction 定位为 ML 任务，但工业界大量使用 log parsing 和 pattern matching 来判定 test verdict（尤其在复杂 CI 系统中），如 LogParse 系列工作。\n2. **Code agents with execution feedback**: SWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024) 和 OpenHands (Wang et al., 2024) 等 code agent 使用 execution feedback（包含 exception traces）进行 iterative debugging，与本文的 \"exception as diagnostic signal\" 直接相关但未讨论。\n3. **Selective context / input pruning for LLMs**: 论文的 \"information density\" 主题与 selective context 文献密切相关（如 Li et al., 2023 \"Compressing Context for Enhanced Language Model Performance\"），但 Related Work 仅在 Training Efficiency 段落间接提及。\n\n---\n\n## 引用验证结果\n\n通过 OpenAlex 自动核查 54 条引用：\n- **39 条已验证**（title + year 匹配）\n- **8 条未在 OpenAlex 中找到**（主要为 2025-2026 年新论文：chen2025tracepile, eguchi2025etcot, ferrando2025execute；以及 API 索引问题：wong2014dstar, kang2024autofl, dinella2022toga 等——这些是已知的 SE 会议论文，属于 API 覆盖限制而非虚假引用）\n- **7 条有轻微 mismatch**（作者名编码差异：如 Rozière vs Rozi\\`ere, Spieß vs Spiess）\n- **结论：无虚假引用证据**\n\n---\n\n## 主要优势\n\n1. **实验设计严谨**：4 个模型、3 个架构家族、多种子验证（exception_only 3 seeds × 4 models），所有结果配有 Wilson 95% CIs 和 paired bootstrap tests。这在 code LLM 领域的实证研究中属于高标准。\n2. **消融设计全面**：7 个 trace conditions + format marker ablation + loss ablation + budget sweep + truncation direction comparison，系统性地隔离了各个变量的贡献。\n3. **Limitations section 诚实详尽**：列出 8 项限制，包括 seed variance、generator-evaluator overlap、self-familiarity bias 等，展现了良好的学术自觉。\n4. **信息密度分解框架**：gradient dilution vs information overload 的分解（Section 3.4）虽然仅在单一模型上验证，但概念上有新意，为理解 \"为什么 verbose input 降低性能\" 提供了定量框架。\n5. **Budget curve 和 phase transition 分析**（Section 3.5, Appendix I）：跨 4 个模型的 tail-truncation budget sweep 清晰定位了 ~500 token 的信号窗口，这是一个可复现的实验发现。\n6. **Regex baseline 系列**（Table 7, Appendix P）：6 个 regex baselines + nomarker ablation 有效解决了 \"模型是否只是学了格式信号\" 的问题。\n\n---\n\n## 格式合规检查\n\n| 项目 | 状态 |\n|------|------|\n| 正文 ≤ 8 页 | ✅ Section 6 (Conclusion) 在第 8 页结束 |\n| Limitations section | ✅ 详尽（8 项） |\n| Ethics Statement | ✅ 含计算资源和社会影响声明 |\n| 匿名 | ✅ \"Anonymous ACL submission\"，无暴露作者身份的线索 |\n| [review] option | ✅ `\\usepackage[review]{acl}` (main.tex line 2) |\n| ARR Checklist | ✅ 作为独立文件 (arr_checklist.tex) |\n| 代码/数据链接 | ✅ 未包含（\"will be released upon acceptance\"） |\n| 参考文献格式 | ⚠️ 基本一致，但有少量 bib key 与 year 不匹配（如 qwen2025coder → year=2024） |",

Let me carefully analyze Reviewer 1's opinions and compare with my own review. I need to respond to each point with [AGREE] or [REBUT], and address the three specific divergence points raised by the Director.

Let me go through R1's points systematically:

**R1's Must-Fix:**
- N1: Wilson CI independence assumption with 48.99% duplicates
- N2: ae_only/loop_only ablation only on Qwen-7B (I also raised this as W2)


**R1's Should-Fix:**
- W1: DeepSeek seed 123 selective reporting
- W2: 24%/76% causal decomposition overclaim (I also raised this as W1)
- W3: CodeLlama tail-2048 collapse
- W4: DebugBench insufficient as cross-dataset validation
- W5: Generator-evaluator overlap

Now I'm working through each concern. On the Wilson CI independence issue, R1 has a legitimate statistical point—the paper treats 1190 trials as independent when nearly half are duplicates, which would artificially narrow the confidence intervals and overstate precision.

But looking at what the paper actually provides, they've already addressed this: they ran a deduplication sensitivity analysis showing zero accuracy change across all conditions, and they report the deduplicated CI in the appendix with the effective n=607. The wider CIs under deduplication wouldn't alter the main conclusions since the accuracy gaps between models are substantial, though it does matter for the tighter comparisons like the exception_only versus ae_only results.

R1 has a fair point about reporting rigor—the main text should ideally specify the bootstrap was done at the problem level rather than leaving readers to discover this in the appendix. Since the dedup sensitivity shows no impact on findings, this feels more like a methodological transparency issue than something that invalidates the results.

On the tier hierarchy concern, I flagged this as well in my review. The paper does scope Contribution 4 explicitly to Qwen-7B and acknowledges that verifying the pattern on other models is future work, so there's transparency about the limitation. The Discussion's design suggestion does venture beyond what's demonstrated, but the contribution itself is appropriately bounded.

Now let me look at what the paper says about DeepSeek's selective reporting. paper does include caveats about the decomposition being approximate and the label-only loss changing multiple optimization dynamics, but these nuances are buried in Section 3.4 while the Abstract and Conclusion present the findings more definitively—R1 has a fair point here. On the CodeLlama tail-2048 collapse, the paper does acknowledge it's a LoRA instability issue specific to that variant and excludes it from broader analysis, which is a reasonable approach to a legitimate robustness concern.

For DebugBench, I see R1's point about the ceiling effect limiting what we can conclude, but the paper itself is cautious—it acknowledges the narrow margins aren't sufficient to independently validate trace importance and only claims the component ranking is preserved. The cross-dataset validation does feel weak though. On the generator-evaluator overlap concern, that's something I flagged as a minor issue as well.

Looking at where R1 and I diverge on scoring, the gap comes down to what we weight most heavily. R1 emphasizes statistical rigor problems, while I'm more concerned about the fundamental novelty question and the motivation gap between what the paper claims to do and what it actually demonstrates. Both are valid critiques, but I think the novelty issue is more consequential for an acceptance decision, so I'm comfortable staying at 3.0 even though R1's points have some validity.

On the training dynamics analysis specifically, it's genuinely one of the stronger empirical findings—the convergence patterns are interesting. But there's a fairness issue in how the comparison is set up: the exception-only approach gets a massive advantage from the input length difference (around 150 tokens versus over 2000), which makes it hard to isolate whether the improvement comes from the method itself or just from having less noise to process. And there are some inconsistencies in how the results are presented that muddy the interpretation.

For R1's concern about Wilson CI independence, the dedup sensitivity analysis showing essentially zero change is actually pretty reassuring. The confidence intervals would be wider with the smaller sample, but given how large the effect sizes are (18+ percentage points), the core conclusions still hold up. It's worth flagging as something to fix in the main text, but it's not a fundamental problem with the work.

20	\begin{abstract}
21	Execution traces are increasingly used to enhance code language models, yet more trace information does not mean better performance.
22	We present the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails) across four models, three architecture families, and a 1.5B--13B parameter range.
23	Exception events alone achieve ${\geq}$99.83\% accuracy on three of four models (DeepSeek-6.7B 3-seed mean 96.58\% due to one seed exhibiting format collapse), while complete traces plateau at 82--88\% despite containing strictly more information.
24	Training dynamics reveal the mechanism: \texttt{exception\_only} converges to 99.33\% within 50 training steps, while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates across the entire training (82--89\%) without stable convergence, a signature of overfitting to spurious patterns in verbose content.
25	The performance gap approximately decomposes into information overload (${\sim}$76\%) and gradient dilution (${\sim}$24\%).
26	A tail-truncation budget sweep reveals a phase transition at ${\sim}$500 tokens, and even on silent logic errors (55.5\% of failures), \texttt{exception\_only} maintains 100\% recall because test assertions generate exception events.
27	These results show that information density, not information quantity, determines learning efficiency for trace-based verdict prediction: a compact exception event (median 150 tokens) outperforms traces 10$\times$ longer across all tested scales.
28	\end{abstract}

37	\section*{Limitations}
38	
39	Our study has several limitations.
40	First, our primary experiments use a single dataset (591 problems from HumanEval and MBPP-sanitized); while a cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}) confirms that exception dominance generalizes to synthetically injected bugs, generalization to other languages, larger codebases, or real-world fault distributions remains untested.
41	Second, while we evaluate four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters across three architecture families, all are code-specialized; generalization to general-purpose models or larger scales remains untested.
42	Third, DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} exhibits seed-dependent variance: 2/3 seeds achieve 99.33\% while seed 123 yields 91.09\% ($\sigma{=}4.76$pp, $n{=}3$), which we hypothesize reflects LoRA initialization sensitivity in DeepSeek-Coder, though direct evidence is lacking (fail recall = 70.5\% for the outlier vs.\ 100\% for others).
43	Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} shows perfect seed robustness ($\sigma{=}0$, $n{=}3$), but Qwen \texttt{ae\_only} also exhibits seed variance ($\sigma{=}$0.40pp; seed 123 = 99.08\% vs.\ seeds 42/456 = 99.92\%), though far smaller than DeepSeek's ($\sigma{=}$4.76pp).
44	Whether training stabilization techniques can eliminate DeepSeek's seed sensitivity is unexplored; other conditions use a single seed.
45	Fourth, the initial DeepSeek \texttt{full\_trace} run was invalidated by context overflow; a re-run with extended context yields 79.16\% (CI [76.80\%, 81.30\%]), 2.60pp below Qwen (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}).
46	Fifth, the candidate solutions were generated by Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, which also serves as one of our evaluation models; this does not affect verdict prediction but may influence the pass/fail distribution.
47	Sixth, self-familiarity bias may inflate absolute accuracy: both Qwen-2.5-Coder and DeepSeek-Coder were likely exposed to HumanEval and MBPP solutions during pretraining, so the models may partially recognize solutions rather than purely reasoning from trace signals; our cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.
48	Seventh, the error distribution in our test set may not reflect real-world fault distributions: exceptions (especially \texttt{TypeError}, \texttt{ValueError}) dominate LLM-generated failures, but production code may exhibit a broader spectrum of silent logic errors where no exception is raised, potentially reducing the effectiveness of exception-based verdict prediction.
49	Finally, our analysis is limited to verdict prediction; whether exception dominance extends to other classification tasks or generation tasks is an open question.

[review])\n\\usepackage{times,latexsym}\n\\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb}\n\\usepackage{graphicx}\n\\graphicspath{{../../figures/paper/}}\n\\usepackage{booktabs}\n\\usepackage{multirow}\n\\usepackage{xcolor}\n\\usepackage{algorithm}\n\\usepackage{algorithmic}\n\n\\title{Exception Events Are All You Need: \\\\Component Ablation for Trace-Based Verdict Prediction}\n\\author{Anonymous ACL submission}\n\n\\begin{document}\n\\maketitle\n\n\\begin{abstract}\nExecution traces are increasingly used to enhance code language models, yet more trace information does not mean better performance.\nWe present the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails) across four models, three architecture families, and a 1.5B--13B parameter range.\nException events alone achieve ${\\geq}$99.83\\% accuracy on three of four models (DeepSeek-6.7B 3-seed mean 96.58\\% due to one seed exhibiting format collapse), while complete traces plateau at 82--88\\% despite containing strictly more information.\nTraining dynamics reveal the mechanism: \\texttt{exception\\_only} converges to 99.33\\% within 50 training steps, while \\texttt{full\\_trace} oscillates across the entire training (82--89\\%) without stable convergence, a signature of overfitting to spurious patterns in verbose content.\nThe performance gap approximately decomposes into information overload (${\\sim}$76\\%) and gradient dilution (${\\sim}$24\\%).\nA tail-truncation budget sweep reveals a phase transition at ${\\sim}$500 tokens, and even on silent logic errors (55.5\\% of failures), \\texttt{exception\\_only} maintains 100\\% recall because test assertions generate exception events.\nThese results show that information density, not information quantity, determines learning efficiency for trace-based verdict prediction: a compact exception event (median 150 tokens) outperforms traces 10$\\times$ longer across all tested scales.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n\\input{introduction}\n\\input{method}\n\\input{experiments}\n\\input{discussion}\n\\input{related_work}\n\\input{conclusion}\n\n\\section*{Limitations}\n\nOur study has several limitations.\nFirst, our primary experiments use a single dataset (591 problems from HumanEval and MBPP-sanitized); while a cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench (\\S\\ref{sec:debugbench}) confirms that exception dominance generalizes to synthetically injected bugs, generalization to other languages, larger codebases, or real-world fault distributions remains untested.\nSecond, while we evaluate four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters across three architecture families, all are code-specialized; generalization to general-purpose models or larger scales remains untested.\nThird, DeepSeek \\texttt{exception\\_only} exhibits seed-dependent variance: 2/3 seeds achieve 99.33\\% while seed 123 yields 91.09\\% ($\\sigma{=}4.76$pp, $n{=}3$), which we hypothesize reflects LoRA initialization sensitivity in DeepSeek-Coder, though direct evidence is lacking (fail recall = 70.5\\% for the outlier vs.\\ 100\\% for others).\nQwen \\texttt{exception\\_only} shows perfect seed robustness ($\\sigma{=}0$, $n{=}3$), but Qwen \\texttt{ae\\_only} also exhibits seed variance ($\\sigma{=}$0.40pp; seed 123 = 99.08\\% vs.\\ seeds 42/456 = 99.92\\%), though far smaller than DeepSeek's ($\\sigma{=}$4.76pp).\nWhether training stabilization techniques can eliminate DeepSeek's seed sensitivity is unexplored; other conditions use a single seed.\nFourth, the initial DeepSeek \\texttt{full\\_trace} run was invalidated by context overflow; a re-run with extended context yields 79.16\\% (CI [76.80\\%, 81.30\\%]), 2.60pp below Qwen (Table~\\ref{tab:cross_model}).\nFifth, the candidate solutions were generated by Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, which also serves as one of our evaluation models; this does not affect verdict prediction but may influence the pass/fail distribution.\nSixth, self-familiarity bias may inflate absolute accuracy: both Qwen-2.5-Coder and DeepSeek-Coder were likely exposed to HumanEval and MBPP solutions during pretraining, so the models may partially recognize solutions rather than purely reasoning from trace signals; our cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.\nSeventh, the error distribution in our test set may not reflect real-world fault distributions: exceptions (especially \\texttt{TypeError}, \\texttt{ValueError}) dominate LLM-generated failures, but production code may exhibit a broader spectrum of silent logic errors where no exception is raised, potentially reducing the effectiveness of exception-based verdict prediction.\nFinally, our analysis is limited to verdict prediction; whether exception dominance extends to other classification tasks or generation tasks is an open question.\n\n\\section*{Ethics Statement}\n\nThis work uses publicly available benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP-sanitized, DebugBench) and does not involve human subjects, crowdsourced annotations, or personally identifiable information.\nAll models evaluated are open-source and publicly accessible.\nTraining uses parameter-efficient LoRA fine-tuning on two RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with each experiment using a single GPU.\nTotal compute is approximately 320 GPU-hours across all conditions, models, seeds, and iterative refinements (including approximately 170 hours for successful experiments; individual runs range from 0.5h for small models to 2.2h for CodeLlama-13B, with the total reflecting 4 models $\\times$ multiple conditions $\\times$ multiple seeds $\\times$ iterative development).\nWe do not foresee direct negative societal impacts from this work; verdict prediction is a developer-facing tool for automated testing.\n\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\appendix\n\\input{appendix}\n\n\\end{document}\n",

      "totalLines": 65
    }

250	\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
251	\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}
252	
253	The VOTA cross-model gap (14.96pp, Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}; confounded by tokenizer-driven truncation; 91.7\% of DeepSeek training samples were affected) is driven by a training-time truncation asymmetry.
254	The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
255	The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
256	
257	A post-hoc group analysis provides directional evidence: partitioning DeepSeek VOTA test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}0.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
258	Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) confirms that DeepSeek VOTA achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}, in contrast to Qwen VOTA, which achieves 100\% fail recall.
259	
260	Seed robustness diverges across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), while DeepSeek shows bimodal behavior: seeds 42 and 456 achieve 99.33\% (fail recall = 100\%), seed 123 yields 91.09\% (fail recall = 70.5\%).
261	Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).
